nodes.label: Introduction to Information Security
nodes.description: Core foundational principles of the CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability), security policies, threat vectors, and risk assessment.

nodes.label: Cryptography Basics
nodes.description: Foundational cryptosystem concepts including plaintext, ciphertext, cryptographic keys, algorithm transparency, and Kerckhoffs's principle.

nodes.label: Symmetric Encryption
nodes.description: Cryptographic primitives sharing a single secret key for both encryption and decryption, including block ciphers (AES) and cipher modes (CBC, GCM).

nodes.label: Cryptographic Hash Functions
nodes.description: Deterministic one-way mathematical algorithms producing fixed-size digests with pre-image resistance and collision resistance (e.g., SHA-256, HMAC).

nodes.label: User Authentication
nodes.description: Identity verification schemes utilizing credentials, salted password hashing, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and signed bearer tokens.

nodes.label: Access Control
nodes.description: Authorization frameworks governing resource access based on identity and privileges, including Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), ABAC, and the Principle of Least Privilege.

evidence.sentence: Information security goals of confidentiality and integrity require cryptosystem fundamentals.
Before studying ciphers, students must master threat models and security objectives.
Symmetric algorithms apply basic cryptosystem primitives using a shared secret key.
Understanding key spaces and plaintext blocks is required before studying AES.
Cryptographic hash functions provide one-way transformation without a decryption key.
Message integrity verification builds on mathematical cryptosystem definitions.
Secure password authentication requires salting and cryptographic hashing via SHA-256 or bcrypt.
Challenge-response authentication protocols utilize keyed hash functions (HMAC).
Authentication tokens and session cookies require symmetric encryption for confidentiality.
Access control models determine authorized permissions only after user identity is authenticated.
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) binds verified user accounts to specific organizational roles.
